After World War II the wartime alliance between the United States and the Soviet Union broke down, and the Truman Doctrine of 1947 committed the country to containing communism. In the years that followed the Soviets tested an atomic bomb in 1949 and China became communist, so many Americans felt the world was getting more dangerous, and this fed worries at home about spies and subversion.

Fear was an important force shaping how Americans responded inside the country, but it was not the only one, because politics and pride in American success also mattered. Fear explains the loyalty investigations and civil defense, while competition and confidence explain the push for science.

The documents show fear in the early Cold War. In Document 1, Doris Kemble writes that her office had to fill out long forms listing every club she ever joined. She says a coworker worried about a theater group from 1938 and that she stopped signing petitions. This shows that loyalty checks made ordinary workers afraid to speak or join anything. Document 3 is a civil defense pamphlet from 1955. It tells families to build a basement shelter, store water and food, and have children drop under their desks in school drills. This shows that people were told an attack was possible and had to get ready for it, although the pamphlet also says panic is the enemy's best weapon.

Fear was not everything, though. In Document 4 a physics teacher says that after the Russian satellite went up, parents wanted more physics classes. But he says this is not a matter of panic, it is a matter of whether we intend to lead. So he is asking for money for modern equipment and better teachers because he wants America to compete and win. This is more about confidence and ambition than fear. Sputnik was a shock, but the response was to improve schools.

Outside the documents, the National Defense Education Act of 1958 gave federal money for science, math and foreign language education. This shows that the government answered Sputnik by investing in schools, which fits the teacher's argument that the response was about leading and not only about being scared. Likewise the Army-McCarthy hearings in 1954 and the Senate censure of Senator Joseph McCarthy later that year show that fear of communists did not last forever and that many Americans turned against the extreme investigations.

In conclusion, fear was a major force in the early Cold War, especially in the loyalty investigations and the civil defense drills, but it was not the primary force by itself. Over time, a desire to compete with the Soviets and improve American education became just as important, so fear was one cause among several.

input.essay:
Before 1763, the British colonies in North America had mostly governed themselves. Under salutary neglect, Parliament rarely enforced trade laws like the Navigation Acts, and colonial assemblies such as the Virginia House of Burgesses got used to controlling taxes and local affairs. Colonists had also read Enlightenment writers like John Locke, who argued that government rests on the consent of the governed and exists to protect natural rights. When Britain came out of the Seven Years' War deep in debt and started passing laws like the Sugar Act and the Stamp Act, colonists saw this as an attack on rights they thought they already had. This background matters because it shows the Revolution started as a defense of self-government, not a plan to remake society. Because of that, the American Revolution greatly changed political life by replacing monarchy with republican government based on consent, but it changed social life much less, since women, enslaved African Americans, and Native Americans were mostly left out of its promises until later Americans used its own language to demand more.

The biggest change was political. Americans rejected the idea of a king and built governments on written constitutions. The new states wrote constitutions in the 1770s, and many of them included bills of rights and gave more power to elected legislatures because people feared a strong executive like George III. At the national level, the Articles of Confederation created a weak government with no power to tax, and after problems like Shays' Rebellion, leaders wrote the Constitution in 1787. The Constitution set up a republic with separation of powers, and the Bill of Rights in 1791 protected freedoms such as speech, press, and religion. Some states also widened voting by lowering property requirements. These were real changes, because ordinary white men now had more say in government than they had under British rule.

Socially, though, the change was much more limited. Women could not vote in almost every state, and the idea of republican motherhood said women's role was to raise virtuous sons for the republic. This gave women some new respect and more support for their education, but it still kept them in the home. Slavery was an even bigger contradiction. Northern states such as Pennsylvania passed gradual emancipation laws, and the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 banned slavery in the Northwest Territory, so the Revolution's ideas did put some limits on slavery. But the Constitution protected slavery through the three-fifths clause and the fugitive slave clause, and slavery grew in the South after the cotton gin. For Native Americans the Revolution was worse, because with Britain gone, settlers pushed west faster onto their land.

Still, the Revolution's ideals ended up mattering over the long run because later groups used them to push for changes the founders never made. At Seneca Falls in 1848, reformers wrote the Declaration of Sentiments, which copied the Declaration of Independence but said "all men and women are created equal." Abolitionists like Frederick Douglass also pointed to the Declaration to show how hypocritical slavery was. After the Civil War, the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery, the Fourteenth gave citizenship and equal protection, and the Fifteenth banned denying the vote based on race. These amendments came close to applying Revolutionary ideas to African Americans. However, when Reconstruction ended in 1877, Southern whites took back control, and many of these rights were ignored, so the change was again only partly carried out.

In conclusion, the American Revolution was a major political turning point because it set up a republic based on consent and written rights. Its social effects were much smaller at first and mostly helped white men. The ideals it created were still powerful, and over time women and African Americans used them to demand equality, even if by 1877 that equality was still incomplete.

After World War II the alliance between the United States and the Soviet Union fell apart quickly. Soviet control over Eastern Europe led President Truman to adopt containment, announced in the Truman Doctrine in 1947, which promised aid to nations resisting communism. Then in 1949 the Soviets tested an atomic bomb and Mao's Communists won the civil war in China, and in 1950 the Korean War began. These events made the Soviet threat seem close and real, and Americans at home reacted to it in many ways. Fear was the main force shaping domestic responses in the late 1940s and early 1950s, especially in loyalty investigations and civil defense, but it was never the only force, since politicians used fear for partisan gain, and by the late 1950s competition and national confidence in American prosperity shaped responses as much as fear did.

In the early years fear of subversion clearly shaped how ordinary Americans behaved. Doris Kemble's letter to her brother in 1947 (Document 1) describes Truman's loyalty order and coworkers worrying about clubs they joined years ago, and a woman investigated over French fashion magazines. Because this is a private letter to family and not meant for the public, it is a good sign of real fear, since Doris has no reason to exaggerate. She has even stopped signing a petition for a playground and is afraid her mail is being read. This shows fear was causing people to limit their own freedoms.

However, fear was also used on purpose by people with political goals. The Granger Falls Courier editorial (Document 2) lists the Soviet bomb, the fall of China, and the conviction of a former State Department official to argue that concern about subversion is not hysteria. But the paper is Republican-leaning and written in 1950, an election year, and it tells voters to "remember in November" which candidates took the danger seriously. Its purpose is to attack the Democratic administration, so the fear it expresses is partly a political tool. This matches Senator Joseph McCarthy, who in 1950 claimed to have a list of communists in the State Department and gained national power through fear until the Army-McCarthy hearings in 1954 turned the public against him and the Senate censured him.

Civil defense also shows fear, but in a controlled way. The Marlow County pamphlet (Document 3) tells families to build basement shelters and describes school duck and cover drills. Still, the pamphlet's purpose is to prevent panic, saying "a prepared citizen is a confident citizen." Officials wanted to turn fear into confidence so the nation would not be "blackmailed."

By the late 1950s responses were shaped more by competition than pure fear. After Sputnik in 1957, the physics teacher in Document 4 says parents suddenly want more science classes, but he insists "this is not a matter of panic" but of whether America intends "to lead." Since he is testifying to get money from the legislature, he has a reason to frame it as leadership rather than fear, but the results were real. Document 5 shows physics enrollment in Linwood County rising from 380 in 1958 to 720 in 1962, with chemistry and math rising too, which fits with the federal money from the National Defense Education Act of 1958. Even so, this is only one suburban county.

Prosperity also gave Cold War attitudes their confidence. The historian in Document 7 argues that the suburban home and full refrigerator, shown in the 1959 Kitchen Debate, were seen as proof that capitalism was better, and this was "not mainly a story of fear." He also points out that Black families and poor Americans were left out, so the showcase had limits.

Finally, some Americans pushed back against fear itself. Agnes Whitcomb's 1961 letter (Document 6) criticizes fallout shelter salesmen and a neighbor with a rifle, and worries about strontium-90 in children's milk. She refuses to accept "more fear" and calls for a test ban treaty. Her pressure, along with others, helped lead to the Limited Test Ban Treaty in 1963.

Overall, fear was the strongest force early in the Cold War, but it was mixed with politics, competition, prosperity and dissent, and over time confidence and competition became just as important.
